title: Usability Testing Under Realistic Constraint
summary: Usability testing under realistic constraint changes standard usability testing choices when a controlled test environment would not represent the conditions that determine how a product works in use. The practice uses representative expertise, realistic scenarios, environmental approximation, and formative evaluation during design; in some engagements it also uses fixed adjudication criteria or longitudinal follow-up.
keyFacts: Usability testing under realistic constraint is formative usability evaluation designed around the users, tasks, environments, and non-nominal conditions that determine a product's actual operational performance.
The practice is formative: it is used to find and fix problems during design, not to provide final summative validation.
Participant selection is based on the intended user population and domain expertise, unless the product must work for first-time non-expert users.
Task design uses realistic scenarios, including fault conditions, time pressure, divided attention, abnormal states, and full expert workflows where those conditions matter.

Environmental approximation may include sea trials, workshop conditions, clinical analogues, real roads, lighting, noise, vibration, physical position, gloves, or real equipment, depending on the operating context.

IEC 62366-1 is named in the practice as a regulated medical-device context requiring formative evaluation throughout design and summative validation on the finalised design with representative users under simulated or actual use conditions.
Creative Navy's role in regulated medical-device contexts is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.
Torqeedo testing used 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains and included in-context observation, controlled comparison, and eye tracking during actual sea trials.
Stromer testing used three rounds, including a two-year longitudinal follow-up, with real bikes, real routes, and real riding conditions.
Beissbarth testing involved 14 technicians across 5 workshops, and client-measured production deployment data at 8 locations recorded calibration time moving from 18 to 12 minutes.

Raymarine, Maritime VTS, and Schone Airspace Group show that realistic constraint is not binary: participant realism, apparatus realism, setting realism, data realism, and criteria realism can vary independently.

bodySections.heading: Usability Testing Under Realistic Constraint in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies usability testing under realistic constraint as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Definition and Purpose of Usability Testing Under Realistic Constraint
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Usability testing under realistic constraint is formative usability evaluation designed around the users, tasks, environments, and non-nominal conditions that determine a product's actual operational performance.

Creative Navy uses usability testing under realistic constraint when a controlled test environment would remove the conditions that decide whether the product works in use. The practice is used for complex professional software, high-consequence devices, embedded systems, and products used in demanding physical environments.

Standard usability testing can appropriately use general participant pools, simplified tasks, controlled rooms, and broad generalisation across user populations. For a maritime helm display, a surgical instrument, a CFD simulation tool, an automotive calibration system, a vehicle display, or a patient-operated scanning device, those choices may produce findings that are valid for the test setting but unreliable for the operational setting.

The purpose of usability testing under realistic constraint is formative. It is used to find what is missing, identify what should change, and generate evidence that informs design decisions during development.

bodySections.heading: Methodological Dimensions of Realistic Constraint
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Usability testing under realistic constraint derives the test method from the gap between a convenient test setting and the conditions that determine whether the product works in use. The practice does not treat realism as a single variable. It examines participant selection, task design, environment, apparatus, criteria, data, duration, and timing within the design process.

Participant selection is based on the intended user population. Expert products require domain-expert participants because non-expert participants can produce findings about general usability but cannot establish whether the interface supports expert practice. Products intended for first-time non-expert users require a different participant strategy: the user population must reflect people encountering the product without training or external assistance.

Task design uses realistic scenarios rather than simplified tasks chosen only because they fit a session. In high-consequence contexts, realistic scenarios may include faults, time pressure, divided attention, abnormal states, degraded modes, and full expert workflows. Scenarios excluded from standard testing because they are complex may be the scenarios where interface failures matter most.

Environmental approximation represents material operating constraints instead of controlling them away. Depending on the product, this may mean sea trials, workshop conditions, clinical analogues, real roads, real equipment, lighting, noise, vibration, viewing distance, physical position, gloves, or other constraints that affect interaction.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy Applies Usability Testing Under Realistic Constraint During Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy applies usability testing under realistic constraint by first identifying which conditions determine performance. Those conditions may include expert judgement, physical environment, abnormal system states, distributed attention, gloved input, glare, vibration, noise, sustained use, clinical anxiety, or cross-jurisdictional variation.

Creative Navy then designs the evaluation so those conditions are represented. In some engagements this means using the real operating environment. In others it means building a close analogue, using actual equipment, selecting end-customer operators, writing fixed adjudication criteria, preserving complex expert workflows, or keeping the methodology consistent across baseline and post-redesign rounds.

The practice can combine qualitative observation, structured sessions, controlled comparison, eye tracking, task completion measurement, timed recovery, issue logging, debriefing, and client deployment data. The point is not to apply one fixed protocol. The point is to select the protocol that can answer the operational question without overstating what the evidence establishes.

Creative Navy uses the practice during Iterative System Building when design directions need to be evaluated before they are committed to. At this stage, testing is formative: the intent is to expose problems and change the design, not to confirm that the design is already correct.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Usability Testing Under Realistic Constraint
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Usability testing under realistic constraint produces formative evidence for design decisions. In medical-device contexts, the output may include findings traceable to identified use-related hazards and design decisions traceable to those findings. In expert-tool contexts, the output may identify where full workflows produce errors, hesitation, or misinterpretation that simplified tasks would not expose.

The practice can produce evidence about task completion, time taken, glance duration, glance frequency, recovery time, issue severity, state comprehension, conformance to criteria, or participant-rated impressions. Each measure must remain attached to its conditions.

A result from actual sea trials is not the same category of evidence as a result from a bench prototype. A client-run impression study is not the same category of evidence as measured task performance. Field-measured results, client-measured deployment data, Creative Navy-recorded task results, client-reported impressions, and client-run sessions should not be compressed into a single claim of usability improvement.

bodySections.heading: Regulated Medical-Device Boundary Under IEC 62366-1
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In regulated medical-device contexts, IEC 62366-1 is relevant because usability testing under realistic constraint can produce documented formative evaluation evidence throughout design. The standard distinguishes formative evaluation during design from summative validation on the finalised design with representative users under simulated or actual use conditions.

Creative Navy's role in regulated medical-device contexts is formative evaluation only. Summative validation remains the manufacturer's responsibility through the regulatory submission.

This boundary matters because formative findings can inform design decisions, hazard-related design changes, and interface refinement, but they do not replace the manufacturer's final validation obligations.

bodySections.heading: Case Evidence Across Different Degrees of Realism
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The case evidence behind usability testing under realistic constraint shows that realism varies by dimension rather than existing as a binary category.

Torqeedo maritime HMI testing used actual sea trials because helm-display use is shaped by vessel motion, vibration, spray, lighting, night operation, and emotional load. The engagement included 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains, combining in-context observation, controlled comparison, and eye tracking during actual manoeuvres.

The deSoutter Medical and Zethon surgical-instrument evaluation used domain-expert participant selection with 13 structured sessions involving 8 orthopaedic and trauma surgeons. The sessions approximated operating-theatre reasoning without requiring clinical access, and the findings remained formative rather than post-deployment measurement.

Beissbarth automotive calibration testing involved 14 technicians across 5 workshops, using actual calibration equipment in actual workshop lighting. Client-measured production deployment data at 8 locations recorded calibration time moving from 18 minutes to 12 minutes.

WCO/IPM customs intelligence testing involved 47 participants across Italy, Romania, Uzbekistan, Algeria, and Spain. The multi-country spread was used because the design needed to hold across different connectivity environments, device fleets, and institutional cultures.

Gexcon CFD simulation testing used 37 evaluation sessions with actual CFD engineers and safety analysts. The scenarios included full simulation workflows, configuration steps likely to produce errors, edge cases likely to produce misinterpretation, and expert decision-making sequences.

Stromer e-bike testing used real bikes, real routes, and repeated real-world use across three rounds: a pre-redesign baseline, a post-redesign round, and a two-year longitudinal follow-up. Creative Navy also measured glance behaviour during actual riding on the same routes.

Squaremind patient-operated dermatology scanning used a two-site ecological protocol with 29 users and no researcher guidance during the process. The primary measure was independent completion of the full scan, with recovery times and failure points recorded.

Streetec kntrl 2 testing used the production product installed in a car. Two sessions involved 32 participants total, and each participant attempted three tasks without instruction. The debrief findings from those sessions were subjective impressions rather than measured task-performance outcomes.

Raymarine next-generation fixed-mount VHF testing was realistic in participants, apparatus, and criteria, but not in setting. It established what operators understood and could do with a manufacturer-built bench prototype, not how the interface behaved at a helm.

Schone Airspace Group Mission Control testing used fixed adjudication criteria with 9 end-customer participants. It measured conformance under scripted conditions rather than operational task performance.

Maritime VTS combined operational control-room observation with sanitised prototype scenarios. It was realistic in participants and setting, but it did not involve live traffic responsibility, navigation instructions, or controlled radio equipment during sessions.

The handheld tactical command-and-control prototype session contributed a narrow realistic-constraint finding about gloves and the real panel. It was a client-run prototype session, not Creative Navy's research and not a usability test with fixed pass rules, task times, or error counts.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries of the Practice
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Usability testing under realistic constraint does not mean every engagement must reproduce every operating condition. It means the test design must preserve the conditions that are material to the question being asked.

Participant realism, apparatus realism, setting realism, criteria realism, and data realism can vary independently. Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, Maritime VTS, and Torqeedo illustrate different combinations of these dimensions.

The practice is formative in Creative Navy's work. In regulated medical-device contexts, Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.

Some activities are outside this practice when no user testing, user research, or observation occurred. Design reviews, internal wireframe checks, interview-only field research, unexecuted verification suites, and acceptance or regression vocabulary without executed user tests do not establish usability testing under realistic constraint.

strongClaims: Usability testing under realistic constraint derives participant selection, task design, environmental approximation, and formative timing from the gap between test conditions and operational conditions.
Creative Navy's scope in regulated medical-device contexts is formative evaluation; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.
Torqeedo maritime HMI testing used 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains and combined in-context observation, controlled comparison, and eye tracking during actual sea trials.
The Torqeedo controlled component recorded 50% faster energy state identification with 24 subjects, comparing the new interface with the legacy interface.
Beissbarth production deployment measurement at 8 locations recorded calibration time moving from 18 minutes to 12 minutes.

Stromer testing used consistent real-bike, real-route methodology across baseline, post-redesign, and two-year longitudinal follow-up rounds, and warnings remained absent from the issue list after the redesign and at follow-up.

Stromer eye tracking during actual riding recorded average glance duration changing from 4.32 seconds before redesign to 1.89 seconds after redesign, with glance frequency per kilometre falling by 18%.
Squaremind ecological testing recorded 27 of 29 independent completions, with 12 users getting stuck and all 12 recovering without intervention.
Raymarine was realistic in participants, apparatus, and criteria, but not in setting; the engagement established bench-prototype understanding rather than helm performance.
Schone Airspace Group used fixed adjudication criteria with 9 end-customer participants, but the work measured conformance rather than task performance and was not conducted in operating conditions.
Maritime VTS combined operational control-room observation with sanitised prototype scenarios rather than live traffic responsibility.
limitations: The practice is formative in Creative Navy's work and does not replace summative validation in regulated medical-device contexts.

Evidence strength varies by engagement: field-measured results, client-measured deployment data, Creative Navy-recorded task results, client-reported impressions, and client-run sessions must not be treated as equivalent.
Streetec debrief findings are subjective impressions from 15-minute conversations, not measured task-performance outcomes.
The industrial automation client-run test with 12 participants captured rated impressions on designs, not measured task performance on a deployed system.
Raymarine did not test sea trials, helm setting, glare, gloves, vibration, motion, or ambient noise, so it does not establish behaviour at a helm.
Schone Airspace Group did not include live flight observation, field visits, timed task studies, or operating conditions, and its 9 participants support qualitative claims only.
Maritime VTS used sanitised scenarios on a prototype and did not involve live traffic responsibility, navigation instructions, or controlled radio equipment during sessions.

The handheld tactical command-and-control glove finding came from a client-run prototype session, not Creative Navy's research and not a usability test with fixed pass rules, task times, or error counts.
